Lesson 2 of 3

Breadth-first and depth-first search

Explore neighbours level by level, or follow one branch before backing up

Deterministic visualsKeyboard readyPractice only
StepsVisualTermsPracticeSources

Understand one step at a time

Read one idea, then continue. Every step keeps its source visible.

01

Start at one node

Start at A. Use outgoing-neighbour order B before C; the only outgoing neighbours of B and C are D and E respectively.

Source AB-S1

02

BFS keeps layers

BFS visits A at distance 0, B and C at distance 1, and D and E at distance 2. With this neighbour order: A, B, C, D, E.

Source AB-S1

03

DFS keeps a path

With B considered before C, DFS follows A, B, D, then backtracks to A before visiting C, E. A different neighbour order can give another valid DFS order.

Source AB-S1

Source excerpt: In this five-node directed graph, A points to B and C, B to D, and C to E. Both searches start at A and consider each node's outgoing neighbours in alphabetical order. BFS visits nodes by edge distance from A; DFS follows one branch before backtracking.

See the relationship

The SVG has a text equivalent and never relies on color alone.

Key terms

BFS

Search layer by layer away from the start.

DFS

Follow one branch as far as possible before backtracking.

Check your understanding

Three short practice questions. Feedback names the source; results are not an official grade.

1. In the diagram, which nodes are directly connected to A?

2. Which order follows BFS from A?

3. When A considers B before C, which prefix follows DFS from A?
